labs: Lab 7.1 — Atomic transfer: two account rows; BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id=1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT; Verify totals unchanged. Then repeat but run ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT after the first UPDATE — show the balances revert. Open two sqlite3 sessions to try overlapping writes and observe the second session's 'database is locked' behavior.

Lab 7.2 — Savepoints: BEGIN; UPDATE ...; SAVEPOINT sp1; UPDATE ...; ROLLBACK TO sp1; COMMIT; Show that only the pre-savepoint change survived. Note savepoints are standard SQL and work the same in Postgres and SQL Server (SAVE TRANSACTION in T-SQL).

Lab 7.3 — Lost-update demo: read a counter value in two sessions, have both add 1 and write back — the counter only goes up by 1. Fix it by wrapping read+write in BEGIN IMMEDIATE; ... COMMIT; so the second session waits. Dialect note: Postgres/SQL Server solve the same problem with row locks or SERIALIZABLE; SQLite's coarse locking makes BEGIN IMMEDIATE the tool.

Lab 7.4 — Isolation vocabulary: read the SQLite transaction docs and write a one-paragraph summary of why SQLite documents no SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL — its locking gives SERIALIZABLE behavior by default. Dialect note: SQL Server defaults to READ COMMITTED; Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED too. Contrast with SQLite in your notes.
